question: On 4 September 2024, Spain’s Minister of the Economy confirmed the appointment of José Luis Escrivá – still a minister in Pedro Sánchez’s Government – as the new governor of the Bank of Spain. The controversial decision means that a serving minister will lead a financial regulator that will have to make decisions about economic policy that he himself approved.

Escrivá is the latest in a long list of members of the government and the PSOE who have been placed by Sánchez in institutions and bodies that should be independent to ensure Spain’s democracy works as it should. Among other cases, a similar situation occurred with the Public Prosecutor’s Office. In light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission investigate whether the recent appointments by the head of the Spanish Government meet the democratic criteria laid down in the EU Treaties?
Given his connection to the current Spanish Government, does the Commission believe that a conflict of interest may arise when the new governor of the Bank of Spain carries out his duties?
Does the Commission believe that one way of ensuring the rule of law is keeping regulatory and oversight bodies and institutions independent from the government?
answer: The independence of the European Central Bank, national central banks and the members of their decision-making bodies is guaranteed at the highest level of EU law (1). Member States are competent to set the conditions for the appointment of central banks’ governors, provided that they respect and maintain the fundamental requirement of central bank independence.
Article 130 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and Article 7 of the European System of Central Banks/European Central Bank Statute.
